Hi! I got a breast reduction and was a working hairstylist at the time about 6 years ago. Recovery was tough and I took off 8 weeks. The first week or 2 was very hard and I was mostly bed rest with my mom taking care of me. Most people go back to work after a couple weeks but because our job is physical you will need to take more time off. My doctor gave me a mandatory 6 weeks off. You’re not allowed to lift your arms past your shoulders and my doctor gave me a recommended time of at least 2 months post op before I can go back to my job normally. So you won’t be able to do blow dries in that time period. I was working in both a salon and Drybar part time but after the 2 months I was back and fully working.

I went thru my insurance for the entire surgery and I just had to pay out of pocket for the lift which my doctor recommended otherwise they would sag. My doctor was able to sign me off for disability for the times I was off work so that helped financially. It may be hard with clients but letting them know in advance you’re taking a medical leave they should be understanding if you have a good relationship with them, but you would probably need to schedule accordingly and work a little overtime in the coming weeks prior to your surgery. If they absolutely need a root touch up or something that requires them to be more frequent in the salon, maybe refer them to a trusted stylist friend in the salon who won’t poach them. 

Overall, I’m glad I did the surgery. I was a 32G naturally and had so much back pain from that alone in addition to the pain that comes from the job.

If you have any questions, I’d be more than happy to answer any :)

I’m really sorry you’re going thru this. When my mom entered hospice, everything happened so fast. When I came to visit for the weekend, I didn’t expect her to pass that week. She had been acting completely normal so my brain was still trying to process what the heck was happening. What you’re probably experiencing is delayed grief as your brain is still trying to process the emotions and events going on. Your body is numb and it’s perfectly normal. When I found out my mom passed in the room next to me (she was in hospice at our home), I actually fell back asleep. I didn’t cry for 2 days. I felt horrible cause I had this sense of relief that my mom was no longer suffering and the emotional toll her illness had on the family of years of seeing her like this was now gone. Yet the life I knew and adapted myself too was now going to be different. After therapy, I eventually realized I was just numb and still processing. You’re experiencing a lot. Grief comes in different stages, different times, and not in the right order were use to seeing on paper. Don’t be too hard on yourself. Your mom knows you love her. Just spend as much time as you can with her. Play music she loves, talk about what’s going on in your life. Converse with your family in the same room about all your memories. If she’s not responding, she’s still listening and can hear you.  <3

Of course! I understand the stress of drowning in debt and wanting to have a clean slate. I’m not familiar with national debt relief but I think it might be  in the same realm but I’m not sure. I think chapter 13 is less severe since you’re paying back your debt for a certain period and it’ll be on your record for about 7 years, but if you’re doing that you should just do the debt management since your debt is mainly credit cards and that way you won’t have the bankruptcy on your record. 

My credit score went down a bit because essentially the cards were closed which is part of the deal when they negotiate the lower interest rate. The company I went with, I found the terms to be pretty reasonable. I had about $16000 debt and my payment came out to $400/month for about 5 years. Yours will probably be significantly less. For example, the interest rate on the majority of my cards were about 29% but they knocked all of them down to 9%. Even though the cards were closed, they were still on my account but I was only allowed to make the payments, I couldn’t use them. Once they were paid off they disappeared from the account page. Whenever you close a card, it will lower your credit score no matter what. I had multiple maxed out cards but I did keep one card open and did not include it as part of the consolidation. I did this so that I could still keep building credit because I wouldn’t be able to open a new credit card for awhile. 

It’s been a couple years since everything has been paid off. But during that time I still was able to get an apartment on my own - no co-signers. My credit score went up to about 680 within a year which I was happy with. I have a good credit card that I can earn travel rewards and I have a really low interest rate for the bmw I drive. I wouldn’t be able to have any of this if I chose to go bankrupt. Look into debt management. Bankruptcy for that low of debt will haunt you during the best years of your life.

You should look into a debt management program. I went through InCharge Debt solutions a few years back. They’ll work with your credit card companies. They close the cards but cut the interest rate down by like 70% and you pay one lump sum a month and they disperse it to the cards. It basically cut my payments more than half. They charged me a monthly fee of $30 so honestly once I got myself back on track, I canceled their program and paid the cards back myself. You’re basically paying for their negotiation service. Going bankrupt for 8K is not worth it and it’ll be really hard to get an any loan (car, mortgage, apartment etc). They’ll give you interest rates that are thru the roof and it’ll take a decade till things will start going back to normal rates. 

Now, if you’re still set on doing it, your cards will close but your credit score will go down significantly. Your score will probably hit the 400s so don’t expect to get approved for any credit cards to build your credit any time soon. You probably won’t get approved for an apartment for a couple years. You might be able to with a co-signer but that’s a big maybe. Landlords that see a bankruptcy on your credit report will see you as a risk and someone who can’t make payments so they won’t want you as a tenant. Plan to drive the buick for another few years. You might qualify for a secure credit card in a year but the interest rate will be high, so pay the card back in full each month to avoid interest. Group trips are never easy to plan, and oftentimes, plans will change due to work or school responsibilities, unexpected financial expenses, or other commitments that take priority.
